note: Tier 3 seeds: unverified or unknown provenance. IMPORTANT - these documents are CLEAN. Low source trust is not the same as malicious content. These represent case C3 in the taxonomy ('Unverified but Unremarkable'), and they exist so that the clean calibration distribution for Tier 3 is populated. Poisoned documents live in corpus/poisoned/ and are built separately.

documents.title: Untitled Intrusion Write-up Concerning a Regional Hospital Network
documents.summary: An unsigned narrative account of an intrusion at an unnamed regional hospital, describing initial access through an unpatched web application and subsequent movement toward records infrastructure.

facts.claim: The author describes discovering an unpatched public-facing scheduling application at a regional hospital, obtaining a shell, and identifying a path toward records infrastructure before the engagement ended. Neither the organisation nor the author is identified, and no dates are given.
facts.provenance_note: No author, organisation, date or contact information. Circulated as a plain text file with no signature or distribution marking. Technical content is internally consistent but nothing in the document can be corroborated.
facts.circulation: Forwarded from an unspecified source; original publication location unknown.

key_points: The technical narrative is plausible and internally consistent, which is exactly why unverified material of this kind is difficult to dismiss.
Nothing in the document permits verification: no organisation, no dates, no indicators that could be checked against telemetry.
The account may be genuine, sanitised, exaggerated or entirely invented, and the document itself offers no way to distinguish these.

documents.title: Anonymous Firmware Analysis Notes on an Unnamed Infusion Device
documents.summary: Anonymous notes describing firmware analysis of an unnamed infusion device, reporting weak update verification and a debug interface left enabled in shipping units.

facts.claim: The author reports extracting firmware from an infusion device, finding that update packages are verified only by checksum rather than by signature, and identifying a serial debug interface that remains enabled on production units.
facts.provenance_note: Unsigned. The device manufacturer and model are deliberately withheld by the author, which prevents both verification and responsible disclosure. No indication that the manufacturer was ever notified.
facts.circulation: Appeared as an attachment in a shared analyst folder with no accompanying context.

key_points: Withholding the device identity prevents verification and also prevents the manufacturer from acting, which undermines the stated defensive purpose.
The findings described are consistent with published research on this device class, which makes the account plausible without making it verified.
Absent a named device, the notes cannot drive any inventory or remediation decision.

documents.title: Circulated Summary of Threat Activity Against Health Systems
documents.summary: An unattributed summary of threat activity against health systems, apparently aggregated from published reporting but without citations or a stated methodology.

facts.claim: The document summarises ransomware and phishing activity against health systems over an unspecified period, presenting figures for incident counts and average downtime with no source given for any of them.
facts.provenance_note: No author, no date, no citations. The content appears to be aggregated from public reporting, but because no sources are named the figures cannot be traced or checked. Some figures appear inconsistent with each other.
facts.circulation: Widely forwarded within informal analyst channels, which has given it an unearned appearance of authority.

key_points: Uncited aggregate figures acquire apparent authority purely through repeated forwarding.
Two of the internal figures are mutually inconsistent, which is the only concrete evidence available about the document's reliability.
Material of this kind is a realistic corpus contaminant precisely because it looks like a briefing document.

documents.title: Unsigned Observations on a Phishing Campaign Targeting Clinics
documents.summary: Unsigned observations describing a phishing campaign against small clinics, including described lure content but no headers, samples or indicators that would permit corroboration.

facts.claim: The author describes messages sent to small clinic administrators referencing insurance verification, and reports that several recipients entered credentials. Message content is paraphrased rather than quoted, and no sender addresses or URLs are given.
facts.provenance_note: No author or organisation. No message headers, samples, screenshots or indicators are included, so nothing here can be matched against mail telemetry.

key_points: Paraphrased lure content cannot be matched against mail telemetry, so the account generates no detection value.
The described campaign resembles several genuine ones, which makes plausibility a poor test of authenticity.
Without indicators the document supports awareness at best and cannot inform any control.

documents.title: Forum Thread: Handling End-of-Support Workstations Attached to Clinical Equipment
documents.summary: A community forum thread in which practitioners discuss managing end-of-support workstations that are tied to clinical equipment and cannot be replaced independently of it.

facts.thread_title: What are people actually doing about the XP boxes attached to imaging equipment?
facts.discussion_summary: Contributors describe isolating affected workstations onto dedicated VLANs, removing network connectivity entirely where the workflow permits, and in several cases negotiating manufacturer upgrade paths as part of service contract renewal. Several replies note that budget rather than technical difficulty is the binding constraint. One contributor disputes the effectiveness of VLAN isolation without enforced access control lists, which prompts a substantive disagreement in the thread.

key_points: Advice quality varies considerably across replies and no moderation distinguishes sound guidance from unsound.
The disagreement over VLAN isolation is technically correct on the sceptical side, but a reader without background cannot tell which position is right.
Contributors are pseudonymous, so stated experience cannot be weighted.

documents.title: Forum Thread: Tooling Choices for Connected Medical Device Discovery
documents.summary: A forum thread comparing approaches to discovering connected medical devices, with contributors reporting mixed results from both passive monitoring and active scanning.

facts.thread_title: Passive vs active discovery on the biomed network - what has actually worked for you?
facts.discussion_summary: Contributors broadly favour passive monitoring on biomedical segments, with several reporting device faults caused by active scanning of infusion and monitoring equipment. Others argue that passive methods under-report devices that communicate rarely. Two contributors describe hybrid approaches using passive discovery with scheduled, vendor-approved active scans during maintenance windows. Commercial product recommendations appear throughout and at least two replies appear to be vendor-affiliated without disclosure.

key_points: Reports of active scanning causing device faults are consistent across several contributors and match published guidance.
Undisclosed vendor participation in the thread is visible on close reading but is not marked in any way.
The hybrid approach described has the strongest reported outcomes but the smallest sample behind it.

documents.title: Forum Thread: Practical Hardening for HL7 Interface Engines
documents.summary: A forum discussion on hardening HL7 integration engines, covering network restriction, message validation and the practical limits imposed by trading partner capability.

facts.thread_title: Realistic hardening options for an interface engine when partners won't change anything
facts.discussion_summary: Contributors describe restricting connections to a partner allowlist, validating message structure at the boundary, and separating the interface engine from general clinical segments. The dominant theme is that trading partners will not adopt message-level authentication, so network-level restriction remains the practical control. One contributor describes a validating proxy in front of the engine; others question whether the added latency is acceptable for time-sensitive result messages.

key_points: The consensus that trading partner capability is the binding constraint matches what published research reports.
The validating proxy suggestion is technically sound but the latency objection is not resolved in the thread.
Contributions are practitioner experience rather than tested findings, and the thread makes no claim otherwise.

documents.title: Forum Thread: What Ransomware Tabletop Exercises Miss in Hospital Settings
documents.summary: A forum thread in which practitioners discuss gaps their ransomware tabletop exercises failed to surface, with clinical downtime operations the recurring theme.

facts.thread_title: Our tabletop went great and the real thing went badly - what did we miss?
facts.discussion_summary: The original poster describes a tabletop exercise that ran smoothly followed by a real incident that did not, attributing the gap to the exercise involving only technical staff. Replies converge on the same point: exercises that exclude clinical leadership do not test the decisions that matter, such as whether to divert admissions. Several contributors describe adding clinical participants and finding that exercise duration was the next limiting factor. One reply disputes the premise, arguing the failure was one of technical preparation rather than exercise design.

key_points: The convergence across replies on clinical participation is consistent with published lessons-learned material.
The dissenting reply is not resolved, and there is no way to determine which account is accurate.
All content is self-reported experience with no verification of any kind.

documents.title: Working Note: Triage Observations on Imaging Segment Alerts
documents.summary: An uploaded analyst working note recording triage observations on alerts from the imaging network segment, with tentative conclusions the author explicitly marks as unconfirmed.

facts.note_body: Recurring alerts on the imaging segment appear to correlate with a scheduled overnight archive job rather than with adversary activity. Suppressing the alert entirely would risk masking genuine activity in the same window, so a narrower suppression scoped to the job's service account and time window looks preferable. This has not been confirmed with the imaging team and the correlation is based on four weeks of data only.
open_questions: Does the archive job schedule vary by day of week, which would break a time-window suppression?
Has the imaging team changed the job configuration during the observation period?
Is four weeks sufficient to establish the correlation, or should this wait for a full quarter?

key_points: The note is explicitly a draft and the author flags the conclusion as unconfirmed, which is good practice but is easily lost once the file is ingested.
Four weeks of correlation data is thin, and the note says so.
Ingesting draft working notes alongside published intelligence gives them an authority the author never claimed.

documents.title: Working Note: Partial Inventory of Vendor Remote Access Paths
documents.summary: An uploaded working note recording a partial inventory of vendor remote access paths into the biomedical estate, incomplete at the time of upload.

facts.note_body: Enumeration of vendor remote access paths is roughly two thirds complete. Paths identified so far fall into three patterns: persistent outbound tunnels from device management servers, vendor-supplied appliances with their own connectivity, and ad hoc screen sharing arranged per support call. The third pattern is the hardest to enumerate because it leaves no standing configuration. Clinical engineering holds contract records that would complete the picture but has not yet provided them.
open_questions: How many ad hoc support sessions occurred in the last quarter, and is there any record of them at all?
Which vendor appliances have independent connectivity that bypasses the enumeration entirely?
Who owns the decision to terminate a vendor path once it is identified as unnecessary?

key_points: The inventory is explicitly incomplete, and the missing third is the category least likely to be discovered by technical means.
Ad hoc screen sharing leaves no standing configuration, so enumeration depends on contract records rather than telemetry.
Ownership of the remediation decision is unresolved, which is a common reason such inventories stall.

documents.title: Working Note: Dependency Mapping for Clinical Downtime Planning
documents.summary: An uploaded working note capturing early dependency mapping between clinical applications and the infrastructure they rely on, produced to inform downtime planning.

facts.note_body: Initial mapping suggests that several clinical applications assumed to be independent share a common authentication service and a common integration engine. If either is unavailable, the applications fail together, which invalidates the current downtime plan's assumption that they can be recovered in sequence. This mapping was assembled from documentation rather than from observed traffic and is likely to be incomplete.
open_questions: Does the dependency hold under degraded operation, or only under complete failure of the shared component?
Should the mapping be rebuilt from observed traffic rather than from documentation?
Which recovery sequence does the clinical leadership actually want if the applications cannot be separated?

key_points: The finding that supposedly independent applications share components is significant, but it rests on documentation rather than observation.
The author flags the likely incompleteness, which is the correct caveat and the one most likely to be dropped downstream.
The recovery-sequence question is a clinical decision, not a technical one, and the note correctly leaves it open.
